The streaming variant of DeepWalk updates vertex representations incrementally as new edges or vertices arrive, rather than requiring the full graph upfront. In the original DeepWalk framework, vertex embeddings are learned from short random walks sampled on a static graph and optimized with a skip-gram objective. The streaming variant adapts this idea to an evolving graph by maintaining and updating the affected local neighborhoods and the corresponding random-walk samples when the graph changes.

Operationally, when a new edge or vertex is observed, the method does not recompute embeddings for the entire graph from scratch. Instead, it updates only the representations of vertices whose local context is altered by the change, typically by generating new or revised walks from the affected region and applying incremental stochastic updates to the embedding model. This makes the method suitable for online or time-evolving settings, because the embedding can be refreshed continuously as the graph grows.

The key idea is that DeepWalk’s neighborhood-based learning is local enough to support partial recomputation: changes in the graph mainly influence nearby vertices, so the streaming variant exploits this locality to reduce update cost while preserving the embedding quality as the graph evolves. In short, it uses incremental random-walk sampling plus localized embedding updates, instead of a full retraining over the entire original network.
